name: Janes special report on Indo-Pacific SOF leaders pushing autonomy and AI
title: Janes special report on Indo-Pacific SOF leaders pushing autonomy and AI
answer: Janes published a September 2026 special report on Indo-Pacific special operations forces leaders calling for faster adoption of autonomy and artificial intelligence. The most useful content is Admiral Frank M Bradley's argument that future operations will involve mass application of autonomous systems, with humans kept on the loop so that only the decisions humans should make are made by them, supported by edge-based cloud-hosted data centres and on-edge laboratories.

sections.body: This is a Janes special report published on 16 September 2026, part of Janes defence intelligence and national security analysis. It covers a meeting of special operations forces leaders from the United States, Canada, New Zealand, Australia, the Philippines, Japan, South Korea, Singapore and Thailand at the Global SOF Foundation's Indo-Pacific Irregular Warfare Symposium in Honolulu from 18 to 20 August 2026. The report is built around remarks by Admiral Frank M Bradley, commander of US Special Operations Command.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: Admiral Bradley told the symposium that the future operating environment would include the mass application of autonomous systems, pointing to the proliferation of uncrewed systems and the emergence of machine learning and artificial intelligence in the Indo-Pacific and globally. He said forces must anticipate and lead in artificial intelligence-enabled man-machine teaming and mass, attritable autonomy. Systems, he argued, should be designed deliberately but able to be adapted at the battlefield edge, with engineers, operators and acquisition staff working together with industry partners before a crisis rather than during one. He called for edge-based, cloud-hosted data centres for special operations units across the theatre, and for on-edge laboratories able to adapt systems at battlefield pace. He also called for abundant, attritable, collaborative autonomous systems across surface, subsurface and air domains on an open, interoperable data architecture. Such uncrewed platforms, he said, should operate collaboratively at scale alongside conventional weapon systems, with humans on the loop so that only decisions humans should make are made by them, and he urged human-machine teaming wherever possible.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The report gives the symposium dates, 18 to 20 August 2026, and the nine participating countries: the United States, Canada, New Zealand, Australia, the Philippines, Japan, South Korea, Singapore and Thailand. Its specific positions come from Admiral Bradley: mass application of autonomous systems in the future operating environment, artificial intelligence-enabled man-machine teaming, mass attritable autonomy, edge-based cloud-hosted data centres, on-edge laboratories, and humans on the loop so that only decisions humans should make are made by them.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: A reader following AI in defense gets a named senior commander's stated requirements rather than vendor claims. Bradley sets out what special operations forces want built: attritable collaborative uncrewed systems across surface, subsurface and air domains, an open interoperable data architecture, edge computing and on-edge laboratories, and human-machine teaming with humans on the loop. It also shows the demand signal is multinational, with nine countries in the room, and that acquisition and industry engagement before a crisis is part of the argument.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Defense

sections.body: The report is a short account of one symposium and one commander's remarks, so it records positions and requirements rather than programmes, contracts or fielded systems. It gives no budget figures, timelines or technical specifications, and no detail on how the described autonomy would be tested or acquired. It is a Janes editorial product behind a subscription, and the claims rest on Bradley's speech rather than independent verification.
